the_question_verbatim: there are probably protocols to work out there about how the callback asks it's host system to hand it whatever data it needs. we might want a common vocabulary there but I don't have any ideas about it.
why_it_gates_something: It decides whether a ground-loop callback is JSON or Python. Akien: 'if it's in python it'll run in the device and can know things about it. but better encapsulation if we can sort how to do this with common nouns and verbs and json.' Python needs no vocabulary — it just reaches for what it wants, and pays for that with arbitrary code in the scan path and no encapsulation. JSON is the preferred answer AND is only possible if the vocabulary exists. So this question is the gate on the format, not a refinement after it.
what_is_actually_being_asked: A callback file sitting in ~/.cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/groundloop/ carries a trigger condition. Evaluating that condition needs data. The data is owned by somebody (Law 6). What is the common set of nouns and verbs by which a declarative callback names the data it needs and gets handed it — without the callback knowing the host's internals, and without the host exporting raw data it owns?
constraints_already_settled_elsewhere: Law 6 — a probe is evaluated wherever its trigger's data is owned. Device-local data is never exported; only the WAKE-UP crosses the bus, never the raw data it tested. (I-heartbeat-probes-and-bus.md, 'Where a probe is evaluated'.)

There is NO CLOSED ENUM of trigger kinds. The shipped interval/date/quantity/state set was already caught as a reification. New signal -> new predicate, NOT a schema change. So the vocabulary must be open at the predicate end while being common at the request end.

advertise -> subscribe -> poke already exists as the registration protocol between a caller and a data-owning device, and it is all bus messages. Whether the callback's data request IS that protocol, or a second thing beside it, is part of this question.
system_rackmount is the owner of host-resource predicates (CPU/memory/disk) and serves threshold probes on request — the one worked example of a device answering somebody else's trigger.
the_tension_to_resolve: A common vocabulary is a closed set by definition, and the trigger kinds are explicitly open. The resolution is probably that the NOUNS (what data, from whom, at what address) are common while the PREDICATE (what counts as true) stays open — but that is a guess and is labeled one (Law 3).
not_answered_here: Akien has no ideas on it yet and said so. CC has not proposed one, deliberately: inventing a vocabulary and handing it back would be the fourth face of words-kept-meanings-replaced, where CC's inference gets recorded as Akien's ruling. This file holds the question open until it is actually answered.
evidence_the_vocabulary_is_reachable: 2026-07-30: the interval use case produces a first common noun without anyone designing one. An interval callback needs a last-fired counter; a Python callback can hold that however it likes, but a JSON callback needs it IN the vocabulary. So 'last_fired' (or its real name) is a noun the use case handed us rather than one invented for tidiness. n=1, and it is the kind of n=1 that suggests the vocabulary can be grown from use cases instead of specified up front.
